body: The new function is pretty nice to read. But there is probably a version with a simple linear search that could work. Not sure its worth investigating though.

definitely style, but I would go with : 
`for (int index=0; index< find_drive_end_idx(*this) ; ++index)`

so all this backtracking part seems unecessary. If I understand correctly (which I may not) we just are looking for special tokens (ie : `./` and `../`). If it is `./` we just skip it basically, without copying it into dest. If it is `../` we just want to remove the portion until the last `/` we found ie ( `C:/super/../` becomes `C:/`). The first case definetly does not need backtracking. You can just compare `if ((*src == '.') && ((src+1) == end || is_path_seperator(*src + 1)) src += 2` which involves no copy. The second one `if ((*src == '.') && ((src+1) < end && (*(src + 1) == '.')  && ((src+2) == end || is_path_seperator(*src + 2))) src += 3` , and you need to save a char* to the last `/` you appended and reset dst to this. If you saved no char yet, then you are in the `// Can't backtrack, so save double dot in the fixed section.`, and you copy them in. If not in those 2 cases, then copy until last separator as you already do. It will save  you some copies.

I would raise a point, as we are in an optimize PR. you can do this with less operations again( but more lines). Here you are doing two `rfind`, but you can do only one reverse loop yourself to find this. No function calls, no max. You can even limit your backsearch to drive_end_idx as a minimum (and not 0)

the if + 2 returns can be squashed into : `return substr(0, MAX(last_separator_idx, drive_end_idx))`

If you did the above change, this can even become  `return substr(0, last_separator_idx)` as you limited the back search to not be smaller.
What do you mean by 'linear search'? I do regret that my implementation always copies the resulting string, even if no adjustments are needed, but such was the case with the old implementation too.
It's a bit confusing to read, I confess, but i'm pretty sure not all compilers are able to optimize the additional `int index` away should I introduce it.

This logic would not work with paths like `path/to/../../`. To avoid copying you will need to forward check the entire string for each path element, to see if it gets removed in the end. This would change its runtime to `O(n log n)` from `O(n)` so it's simply not worth it.
I agree, but before I optimize every situation like that by hand, I'd rather implement `rfind_chars` (on `StrRange`) to not repeat logic, which is definitely outside the scope of this PR.
I mean you are doing multiple find calls. There is _probably_ a way to resolve this in one for loop
Oh, you're right, that works because `substr` already does non-copy logic. Makes sense to me!
What do you mean ? You have a variable in both cases. The two cases should compile to something very similar
I don't know if you'll ever have exactly this case as a function though, bacause you need a reverse find for multiple characters and being able to specify the minimum index. Seems far fetched.

I don't think the complexity will change, but you have a point that you need to store all path separators locations for it to work. If this implies a memory allocation, then there is no point in doing it. Could imagine a static array, but then when a demonic scripts give you back a 2mb path consisting only in `/../../` we will overflow. So I would agree with you to keep it as is.

In the `index` implementation there are two variables (`drive_end_idx` and `index`), in my implementation there is just one (`drive_end_idx`). (besides, for yours there would need to be a line like `int drive_end_idx = find_drive_end_idx(*this)` above the loop to avoid repeating the call for every iteration).
Yeah if you put it above I see your point. Anyway, that's stylistic anyway, and your version is good, so let's resolve this.

I had it implemented with a 'part pos stack' previously because I wanted to avoid backtracking, but the overhead from allocation turned out to be way slower than the overhead from backtracking from most normal length strings - especially since `..` is a rare case.

I think there is a theoretical implementation of this function that uses two passes instead of a stack or backtracking - one forward pass to track the amount of `..` (and whether changes are even needed), and another to apply the changes. But it would use a code (and time) to implement.
The function would be `rfind(StrRange str, StrRange chars)` which i don't think is far fetched at all :)
yeah you are right that would be better. So let's keep that in mind for later. You can resolve this !
